summary:
Ohio is one of sixteen states placed in the second-highest risk tier, "The Worst States," in Erin In The Morning's Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map of July 2026, below the four "Do Not Travel" states. The assessment grades Ohio under a national frame of "Worst Policies In Effect."

Ohio's facility law, Senate Bill 104, the "Protect All Students Act," was signed by Governor Mike DeWine on 27 November 2024 and took effect 25 February 2025. It requires all K-12 schools, colleges and universities, public and private, to designate bathrooms, locker rooms, changing rooms, shower rooms and overnight accommodations for the exclusive use of males or females based on sex assigned at or near birth, with single-occupancy restrooms with controlled use as the only exception. The governor signed the bill out of public view and over the objections of Democrats, teachers' unions and civil-rights groups; the sponsor was Republican state Senator Jerry Cirino. The law contains no enforcement mechanism.

House Bill 8, signed 8 January 2025, requires educators, counselors and other school staff to out LGBTQ students to parents and bars "sexual content," including undefined "gender ideology," from kindergarten through third-grade curriculum, with parental opt-out.

Ohio statutes do not prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity, but gender-identity discrimination in state employment has been barred by executive order since 19 December 2018, and 33 Ohio cities and counties have ordinances barring gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations. The Sixth Circuit held on 7 March 2018 that transgender-status discrimination is sex discrimination under Title VII.

Amendment of the gender marker on an Ohio birth certificate was barred under the 1987 In re Ladrach decision, challenged by four transgender Ohioans in March 2018, and invalidated as unconstitutional by federal Judge Michael H. Watson in Ray v. McCloud in December 2020. Corrections have been officially allowed since 1 June 2021 after no appeal, though some counties continue to refuse them.

Transgender people can change name and gender on Ohio driver's licences via court order and a Declaration of Gender Change signed by a physician, nurse practitioner, social worker, therapist or psychologist, with an X option available since April 2022. In August 2026 the Bureau of Motor Vehicles announced rules allowing only male or female markers and requiring an exact-matching birth certificate or passport.

HB68, the Saving Adolescents from Experimentation Act, passed 13 December 2023, bans puberty blockers, hormones and surgery for under-18s and bars transgender girls and women from women's high-school and college sports. It was vetoed on 29 December 2023, then enacted by House override on 10 January 2024 and Senate override on 24 January 2024. It was blocked in April 2024, allowed to take effect in August 2024 after a court found the regulation of transgender individuals a legitimate state interest, and re-enjoined on 18 March 2025 by the 10th District Court of Appeals, with Attorney General Dave Yost vowing an appeal. The operative position should be checked before travel.

Adult-care rules adopted in January 2024 would have required perpetual psychiatric counseling, an endocrinologist relationship, bioethicist approval and 30-day reporting of gender dysphoria; they were dropped in February 2024.

In January 2024 transgender candidate Vanessa Joy was stripped from the ballot for failing to disclose her deadname under a seldom-enforced law, and three of four transgender state-office candidates were challenged or disqualified.

Same-sex marriage has been legally recognised in Ohio since 26 June 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, invalidating the 2004 Defense of Marriage Act and 2004 Issue 1 constitutional amendment defining marriage as between a man and a woman.

There is no statewide conversion-therapy law after failed bills in 2013, 2015, 2020 and 2021, but seven or more cities ban it for minors, including Cincinnati (December 2015), Toledo, Columbus, Dayton and Athens (2017), Lakewood and Kent (2018), and Cleveland, Cleveland Heights, Akron and Reynoldsburg (2022).
tangentialFactors:
Ohio's placement in the "Worst States" tier sits below the four "Do Not Travel" states (Florida, Idaho, Kansas, Texas), where Idaho's felony bathroom ban carries up to five years and Kansas operates a bounty-hunter civil-suit regime. Ohio's own facility law contains no enforcement mechanism and no criminal penalty, a material difference in day-to-day exposure.

Ohio's facility restrictions apply to schools and colleges rather than to general public accommodations such as restaurants, hotels or shopping centres, so a short-term adult visitor is unlikely to encounter them outside an educational setting.

The Sixth Circuit's 2018 holding that transgender-status discrimination is sex discrimination under Title VII, and Bostock v. Clayton County (2020), give trans workers in Ohio a federal employment-discrimination claim even though Ohio statutes themselves do not address gender identity.
localsOnly:
Ohio's 33 cities and counties with gender-identity non-discrimination ordinances are the practical protection for residents in employment, housing and public accommodations where the state statute is silent.

Gender-identity discrimination in state employment has been barred by executive order since 19 December 2018, and sexual-orientation discrimination in state employment since 21 January 2011.

Birth-certificate gender-marker corrections are officially permitted after 1 June 2021 following Ray v. McCloud, though some counties continue to refuse corrections, so residents may need to shop across counties.

Driver's-licence gender markers require a court order plus a Declaration of Gender Change signed by a licensed clinician; the August 2026 BMV rule restricting markers to male or female with an exact-matching birth certificate or passport narrows the options that had included an X marker since April 2022.

House Bill 8's outing requirement binds Ohio educators, counselors and school staff directly and affects LGBTQ students in the school system year-round.

Local conversion-therapy bans for minors cover Cincinnati, Toledo, Columbus, Dayton, Athens, Lakewood, Kent, Cleveland, Cleveland Heights, Akron and Reynoldsburg, but there is no statewide prohibition.

Ohio recognises same-sex marriage, allows single individuals and married same-sex couples to adopt, provides lesbian couples IVF access, recognises the non-genetic mother if married, and permits surrogacy with enforceable gestational and traditional contracts; there is no second-parent adoption for unmarried couples and no assisted-reproduction recognition beyond marriage, though de facto parents are recognised.

Domestic partnerships for same-sex couples exist in Yellow Springs and in Cuyahoga and Franklin counties, with Cleveland's registry upheld in October 2010.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current operative status of HB68 is unresolved in the sources: the law was re-enjoined on 18 March 2025 by the 10th District Court of Appeals and the attorney general announced an appeal, but no later ruling is sourced here.

Whether the August 2026 BMV marker rule has been challenged in court is not sourced.

Enforcement practice for Senate Bill 104 is not sourced beyond the statute's lack of a stated enforcement mechanism; no reported complaints, investigations or penalties are documented.

Ohio-specific incident data on violence against trans residents, police conduct, or detention conditions is not present in this inventory.

Whether House Bill 8's "gender ideology" curriculum term has been defined by the Ohio Department of Education is not sourced.
